Content: The order of operations is a step-by-step guide for manipulating expressions in algebra. Without it, different people might end up with different answers when simplifying the same complex expression. The order of operations establishes a standardized sequence that ensures a mathematical expression means the exact same thing to every time we work with it.

Algebra problems on the SAT exam often include multi-step expressions and equations, so mastering the order of operations is fundamental. If we simplify algebraic expressions from left to right, we can often end up choosing wrong answer choices designed to catch that mistake. Knowing the order of operations gives us a foolproof method for simplifying even the most intimidating equations and always ending up with the right answer.
A helpful acronym for remembering the order of operations is PEMDAS, which outlines the correct hierarchy of mathematical operations.

:ibox:• Parentheses (and other grouping symbols like brackets or fraction bars) always come first.

• Exponents (and roots) are handled second.

• Multiplication and Division come next. The two operations hold the same level of priority, so we process them from left to right as they appear.

• Addition and Subtraction are the final steps. They share equal priority - just like multiplication and division - and must be worked from left to right.

When solving equations, PEMDAS and the process of “isolating a variable” are actually two sides of the same coin. When given an expression to simplify, we follow PEMDAS strictly in order to shrink the expression into a more concise one. However, when you are given an equation and need to solve for an unknown variable, we can perform PEMDAS in the reverse order. To strip away the numbers surrounding a variable and isolate it, we would undo the addition and subtraction first, then undo any coefficients with the multiplication and division, and finally handle any exponents and parentheses.
